And it's that basically it's that area of land around a river or a stream or a creek that is naturally subject to flooding. And in most places where these streams are undisturbed they're flat so that as the water levels rise it can rise and the water can rise and spread out across that floodplain. It serves to drop out sediment so it can re- it can nourish, replenish is what I'm looking for. The soils in those areas. In urban areas you're not going to see many of these wide floodplains. We've built closer to the streams because everybody likes to have that water access, water view. And so sometimes we've constrained our creeks and streams and they've gotten deeper and wider as we've constrained them so they've become what they call disconnected from the floodplain. But these areas can still flood. And so as we talk about this we also regulate development now that we've seen what over time has happened in some of these areas where we've built in the floodplain. We then regulate an area of land around these creeks and streams. And you may have heard it called the 100-year floodplain or a 1% chance of flood. It's the regulatory floodplain is that land that is subject to a 1% or greater chance of flooding in any given year. The 100-year flood is a little bit deceptive and I think the industry will eventually get away from using that phrase because people tend to think when they hear that well you know I flooded last year so I shouldn't flood again for another 99 years or so. But 1% chance of flood can happen every year. It can happen multiple times a year just depends on what the weather pattern is doing and how much rain you're receiving. We also call a regulatory floodplain a special flood hazard area. That's a FEMA term for it so it's got to have an acronym with it. So it's called an SFHA or a special flood hazard area. And so when you look at Norman, all of these blue areas as well as the red area around the lake, these are the floodplains in Norman. And so you might recognize 10 Mile Flat Creek over here to the west. You can't really see in amongst all the development Brookhaven, Imhoff, Merkle, Bishop but they're all in here. This is the little river that goes down into Lake Thunderbird and then there are other creeks down here like Dave Blue, Jim Blue, Clear Creek that also all feed Lake Thunderbird and are in the Lake Thunderbird watershed. So as part of our requirements through the community rating system or CRS is we have to calculate how many acres are in our special flood hazard area. And so we have 14,865 approximately acres in the city of Norman that are actually in the special flood hazard area. And that's important for our FEMA regulation or FEMA program, our floodplain program. So kind of give you a visual of what a floodplain looks like. That floodplain is this entire stretch. So it's all of this area that's subject to flooding. But you also have pieces in amongst this. So we have in the middle where the channel is and where a majority of the flooding will occur, you have the floodway. And we with our floodplain regulations do not allow development within the floodway because this is where we need to reserve that for normal stream flow. And we have something called the base flood elevation. And again because this is governmental, we've got to have an acronym. So it's called the BFE. And that's the elevation at which water at the 100-year flood will rise. It will rise to that elevation. And so if your foundation, your finished floor on your house is above the base flood elevation, then you're protecting yourself from receiving flooding during the 100-year flood. We actually have what's called freeboard requirements where if you're building within the flood fringe out here, you have to elevate your house two feet above that base flood elevation just as an added measure of protection so that your house is less likely to flood many times in this area. Okay. So with that, we have floodplain management. So basically we have a community program that operates to reduce the risk of current and future flooding. Have zoning, building codes and floodplain ordinances. And then we have a minimum set of floodplain management standards that FEMA sets for us for communities participating in the National Flood Insurance Program or NFIP. And in order to be a CRS community, you have to participate in NFIP. And so we do that. And part of our requirements there are to have a floodplain regulation or floodplain ordinance and to do some certain activities that we'll talk about here in a minute. So one of the things to note with the floodplain is why do we regulate it? Why are we concerned? Well, one of the things is if you're bringing fill material in the form of dirt or houses or other types of materials into the floodplain, you're taking up space where the floodwater would have otherwise resided and causing that water to spread out elsewhere. So before development in this instance where there wasn't the fill in the development here, you can see that this house didn't flood. When you add that fill and you reduce the capacity of that channel of that floodplain, then it pushes the water higher and out and can affect properties that were not affected previously. So that's why when we receive floodplain permit applications that address fill, we restrict fill in the floodplain. They have to provide compensatory storage in order to prevent their upstream or downstream neighbors from being adversely impacted by those activities. So we mentioned the NFIP, the National Flood Insurance Program. It was created by Congress in 1968. It's a program that works to mitigate future flood losses through sound community enforced building and zoning codes. So the important thing to note with this is this is all to prevent future loss. It provides access to affordable federally backed flood insurance protection for property owners and in order for residents and businesses to obtain that flood insurance, the community has to participate in the NFIP and Norman does. So another part of this is the community rating system or CRS. You may have heard through various outreach activities, other presentations that Norman is a CRS Class 6 community. So we'll talk about what that really means and how we got there. But the goal of being a CRS community is to reduce and avoid flood damage to insurable property, strengthen and support insurance aspects of NFIP, and then foster comprehensive floodplain management. So you can see lots of reference to protecting insurable properties and making sure that we adequately manage our floodplain. So with that, communities that choose to participate in CRS, it's a voluntary program, the communities that participate are rewarded for doing more than just those minimum national standards that are set forth by NFIP. So with that, the reward is basically that our citizens receive flood insurance premium discounts based on how many of those efforts and what kind of credit we get for those efforts from FEMA. And those activities can work to reduce flood damage, educate the public on flood data and insurance, and many other things that we'll go through here in just a minute. And so the things that we need to do to get these to become, say, a CRS Class 6 are all spelled out in the CRS handbook. It's a three-inch thick binder full of wonderful language that will help put you to sleep eventually. But it's got very detailed information on many activities that we can undertake as a community in order to increase the discount that our residents receive for flood insurance premiums. So with that, our CRS classification, based on the total amount of credit that we receive for all the activities that we conduct, and right now we are currently a Class 6 community. So the lower the number, the higher the insurance discount. The minimum is a Class 9, and the maximum is a Class 1. And I don't, there are only one or two Class 1s in the entire country. There are only a handful of Class 2s, and Tulsa is actually a Class 2 community. So with that, you can see the amount of points that we have to obtain in order to get those different CRS classes. So a Class 10 is 0 to 499, all the way up to more than 4,500 points to be a Class 1.
